Verb patterns used in #1–#7 are introduced under Choosing Time and Aspect: simple-present base plus -s/-es, simple past including irregular forms, will + base form, am/is/are + -ing, has/have + past participle, and had + past participle.

Patterns used in #8–#10 are introduced under Active and Passive Voice: be + past participle, tense-preserving voice conversion, get + past participle, and nonpassive be/get descriptions. Patterns used in #11–#16 follow the base-form rule and meaning contrasts in Modal Verbs and Meaning.

checked: Base form and past participle are defined before tense and passive patterns need them. The time/aspect section explains each named form alongside its construction.

Subject is explained before active/passive identification. Agent and object are defined before voice conversion needs them. Modal verb, ability, permission, obligation, advice, and possibility are introduced with meaning and examples before the worked tasks.
No mathematical symbols or units need explanation, and no prerequisite teaching is assumed.
Tense is linked to when an event happens and aspect to ongoing action, prior completion, or a present link. Each construction has an explanation of when it is chosen.
Present perfect explicitly explains present result, experience, continuing situations, and events counted in an unfinished period. Past perfect explains completion before a past point.

Voice explains who acts and who receives the action, how to convert both directions, and why passive may be chosen. Get-passive has formation and a reasoned application in #10. Modal sections explain each required meaning; #11–#16 apply them with reasons.

Checked restrictions: no -s/-ed after will, state verbs usually simple rather than progressive, has/have agreement, finished past time versus present perfect, and past perfect not required whenever before establishes order.
Checked voice conditions: ordinary conversion requires an object, agent may be omitted, get-passive is informal, and be/get alone does not establish passive voice.

Checked modal limits: could is described as general past ability, permission varies by formality, must not differs from do not have to, possibility modals overlap, and must can express a conclusion rather than an order.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: Choose the correct form: I think the office *(will close / closed)* early tomorrow.
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: Examples #3, #4, and #5 now work through future will, present progressive, and present perfect selection.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: Tense helps show when something happens.
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: The dense distinction is now split into short sentences with plain descriptions of time and aspect.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: Rewrite the sentence with the correct verb forms: "Yesterday, she walks to the store and bought bread."
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: The correction example now includes an explicit exam-style command.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: A **past participle** is a verb form used after *has, have,* or *had* and in many passive forms.
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: The term is defined before passive formation and includes regular and irregular examples.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: This form can show a present result: "She has finished the report, so it is ready now."
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: Present result, experience, continuing situations, and counts in an unfinished period are all explained and practiced.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: By the time the meeting started yesterday, Ana *(had finished / has finished / will finish)* the report.
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: The revised earlier-completion item offers only one correct option, had finished. Simple past is no longer an alternative key.

language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.quote: **Future meaning with will** uses *will + base form*.
language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.note: Formation and uses are explicit. Example #3 applies future prediction and explains the base-form choice.

language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.quote: It can describe a situation that began in the past and still continues: "She has lived here since June."
language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.note: Formation, present links, and finished-time limits are taught. Examples #5 and #6 apply the distinctions.

language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.quote: Choose the form of *get* to match the time.
language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.note: The get-passive pattern, past form, informal setting, and formal be-passive alternative are taught and applied in #10.

language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.quote: For **ability**, use *can* for present or general ability.
language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.note: Can and could are distinguished for present and general past ability, then applied in #11.

language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.quote: For **permission**, *can* is common in everyday requests.
language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.note: Can, may, and polite could requests are explained. Example #12 applies the formal permission choice.

language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.quote: For **obligation**, *must* and *have to* show a strong requirement.
language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.note: Strong requirement, advice, prohibition, and lack of requirement are contrasted and applied in #13 and #14.

language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.quote: For **possibility**, *may, might,* and *could* can all mean that something is possible: "It might rain later."
language-proficiency-grammar-and-structu.note: Possibility choices and their overlap are explained. Example #15 applies might against a requirement reading.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: Which sentence uses a get-passive: "The package got delivered before noon" or "The package got heavy in the rain"?
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: Examples #8 and #10 distinguish passive actions from be/get descriptions. Example #10 also converts get-passive for formal style.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: 1. *Yesterday* places both actions in past time.
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: The tense-correction solution now uses a numbered list for its reasoning and final rewrite.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: Use it for a prediction, promise, future statement, or decision made as you speak: "I will help you."
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: Will now has explicit selection conditions and a worked prediction example, not just an illustrative form.

lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.quote: It is common in speech and informal writing; use a *be*-passive when a formal style is needed.
lesson-grammar-and-structure-tenses-and-.note: The vague suitable-context condition is replaced with a register distinction and a formal-report application.
